prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: After the first round I keep B020 as the whole prize, but I hold it less firmly than before and I want that to be clear. What persuades me is the structure of the evidence. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011 made a specific, quantitative, falsifiable prediction (flat bands near a magic angle); the 2018 experiments found correlated insulators and superconductivity where the model says the kinetic energy is quenched; and within a decade many independent laboratories have reproduced the phases and carried them to twisted multilayers, transition-metal dichalcogenide moire systems and Chern-insulator physics. Theory and measurement agree on the central structure, and the discovery is a new tunable regime of correlated matter, not a method or a technology milestone. That is the kind of result I trust. The citation can and should be worded around what is established, namely the flat-band prediction and the observed phases, and say nothing about the pairing mechanism. My configuration is unchanged: one part, B020, with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer.
statement.case_against: Three problems remain, and the first round did not remove any of them. First, the credit: Yuan Cao led the 2018 experiments and earlier moire band-structure theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto and others) is not represented, and the three-name limit forces a judgement about group leaders that outsiders will contest. Second, maturity: eight years is short, the pairing mechanism is unresolved, and twist-angle disorder limits quantitative reproducibility from sample to sample. Third, I recognise that B024 has four explicit supporters and is the fallback of three of us, so the committee may reasonably decide that its cleaner two-name credit, quantitative reproduction between laboratories and clear maturity outweigh the novelty argument I make for B020. If the committee cannot defend the credit for B020 as the original work, I would not insist on it.

responses.point: Kroll argues that B024 is the cleanest case on the shortlist: magic-wavelength trapping proposed by Katori, record systematic uncertainty near 1e-18 from Ye's group, reproduction in many laboratories, and a two-name credit. He accepts the lineage objection (2005 comb, 2012 single quantum systems) but does not regard it as disqualifying, and he says the performance figures come from his recollection.
responses.response: I accept his point on attribution and maturity: B024 is better than B020 on both, and I said so in round 1. Where we differ is on what the prize is for. The 2005 and 2012 citations honoured the enabling tools, and I cannot tell from my side whether the magic-wavelength lattice concept is separable from them, so I would ask him and Lindroth to write out in the final discussion why the lattice idea is a distinct achievement and not an excellent application of those tools. If they can, I would be content with B024 as the prize. Since the 1e-18 figures and the clock-to-clock agreement are from memory, I would also support the chair's suggestion that they be checked against the published record before the ballot, because my own support for B024 as a fallback relies on them.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first as a clean idea that created a new capability, and values that the measurements can be confronted with atomic many-body theory (magic wavelengths, blackbody shifts, polarizabilities). She lists incrementalism, a credit tail (SYRTE, PTB, NIST) and unverified priority as reservations, and doubts that fundamental payoffs have yet been delivered.
responses.response: Her argument that clock comparisons confront atomic theory, with magic wavelengths and polarizabilities computed and tested, is exactly the kind of quantitative agreement between calculation and experiment that I value, and it moves me closer to B024. It also sharpens my own reading of the incrementalism point: the promised payoffs she mentions (redefinition of the second, dark-matter or constants limits) are not yet delivered, whereas the moire phases have already been observed. I do not think that settles the matter, but it is the main reason I still hold B020 rather than yield. I would ask her one specific question on credit: does Ye's name rest on the original idea or on record accuracy, because that decides whether the two-name credit is as clean as it is presented.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B051 to B020 and presents the Bistritzer-MacDonald model as a prediction tested by nature, while listing the same maturity and attribution concerns, namely Cao and earlier theory, and saying that B024 is the safer choice if the interpretation is judged unstable.
responses.response: I agree with his framing of the case and thank him for stating plainly what he gave up. On his closing point that B024 is the safer choice if the interpretation is judged unstable, I would make a distinction that I think the committee needs: the unresolved item in twisted bilayer graphene is the pairing mechanism, not the existence and robustness of the correlated and superconducting phases, so a citation limited to prediction and observation does not depend on a settled interpretation. What I cannot defend better than he can is the credit; if we still cannot argue convincingly that MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero did the original work, then the safer course is the one he names and I would vote for B024.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B020 first because of the chain of falsifiable prediction, 2018 experiment and reproduction in many groups, but lists the unresolved mechanism, twist-angle disorder and Yuan Cao's omission, and says B024 is the better-documented alternative if the committee cannot be sure of the original credit.
responses.response: We are close to the same position and I agree that the test for B020 is whether the committee can be sure about the credit for the original experiments. I would add that the answer to the chair's question on Cao is partly a matter of how we word the citation: crediting the discovery of the correlated insulating and superconducting states to the group that led and supervised the 2018 experiments is a defensible, conventional judgement, but it should be recorded as one and not hidden. If she thinks that judgement is not safe, I would like her to say so before the ballot, since that is what would move me to B024.

responses.point: Danielsson now pairs B024 with B019, crediting Halzen alone for IceCube, as a balance between a precision instrument and a discovery about the cosmos, while recognising the attribution of a collaboration-scale result to one person is awkward.
responses.response: I remain sympathetic to the discovery argument for IceCube, but I cannot support a two-part prize in which one part is credited to a single name for a collaboration-scale discovery, and I cannot judge the astroparticle physics myself. If B019 cannot be credited defensibly it should fall away, as he and the chair suggest. I also do not see a way to add B020 as a second part under the three-person limit without cutting its credit to a single name, which would make it weaker, so I treat the choice between B020 and B024 as a choice of one whole prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can defend the three names for B020 as the original work, given Yuan Cao's role in the 2018 experiments and earlier moire band-structure theory.
Whether eight years and an unresolved pairing mechanism make B020 premature, or whether a citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the observed phases is sufficient.

Whether the lattice-clock figures and priority history, which I cannot check from my own field and which colleagues cite from memory, survive verification, and whether the lattice concept is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 citations.
Whether twist-angle disorder and sample variability undermine the quantitative reproducibility of the correlated phases.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B020: my group works on DFT and magnetism, not moire materials, and I have no collaboration or other link to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer. I chaired the 2025 committee, which awarded superconducting circuits, and I have taken that into account in my view of B042, which I do not prefer. Altermagnetism (B050), close to my own work, is not on the shortlist. I note Johansson's disclosed overlap with B042 and have no objection to a recusal ruling on that ballot.
